content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a novel curriculum learning strategy for deep RL called ProCuRL. It is inspired by the concept of Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) used in pedagogy. Authors mathematically derive how to apply the ZPD concept in RL, as well as propose its practical variant that can be incorporated with different RL frameworks. The paper presents experimental results on a variety of domains and demonstrates its effectiveness against other baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

- The paper takes on an important problem in Deep RL, a curriculum learning for agents that are not too hard or too easy. This can provide a natural sequence of tasks for learning quickly on tasks that are always at the forefront of the agent's capabilities.
- This paper provides a comprehensive set of experiments on many domains to illustrate the strong empirical performance of the ProCuRL family of methods.

## Weaknesses

- One of my concerns about this work is the distance between the theory (including the ZPD concept) and the actual practical algorithm used in empirical evaluations.
    - For example, Section 3.2.1. assumes $\theta\in\Theta=[0,1]^{|S_{init}|}$ which is a very big assumption that isn’t held in practice.
    - $PoS^*(s)=1$ is another big simplification that further distances methods from theory and ZPD. What if there are unsolvable tasks in the task space, i.e. the goals are unreachable from a certain initial state? In that case, setting $PoS^*(s)=1$ will provide an incorrect curriculum based on ZSP.
- Another weakness is that all environments seem to include only a limited $|S_{init}|$ (in the order of hundreds, except BasicKernel if I understand correctly). It is therefore unclear how this approach would work if the number of tasks is much larger, perhaps infinite. Would the method scale to such settings?
- It is unclear whether the agents would generalise to new tasks that they have not seen during training. It would be interesting to see the zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization performance of the methods and baselines on environments used for evaluation.
- I’d also be interested to see the curriculum visualisation of ProCuRL-ENV, which is closer to the theory.
- The method proposed in this work presents a great resemblance to some of the Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) methods, which also belong to the field of Curriculum Learning. Specifically, the regret-based UED methods also provide agents with environment variations that are at the frontier of an agent's capabilities [1, 2, 3]. While ProCuRL handles this using curriculum strategy (1), regret-based UED methods use regret (the difference between optimal and current policy) to provide the agent with environment variations to train on (note that regret is very similar to the objective (1) though there are differences, of course). I thus think these connections need to be acknowledged and prior work properly cited.
- (Minor) shouldn’t the $\xi_t$ also include the rewards in their notation?

[1] Dennis et al, Emergent Complexity and Zero-shot Transfer via Unsupervised Environment Design, 2020.

[2] Jiang, et al, Replay-Guided Adversarial Environment Design (2021).

[3] Parker-Holder, et al, Evolving Curricula with Regret-Based Environment Design (2022).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written, clear and easy to follow. The technical quality of the work is high, and theoretical claims are well supported. The way curriculum learning and ZSP are connected are novel, but in a limited way considering regret-based UED methods (see above). The authors provided their code alongside the submission. Therefore, there are no concerns regarding the reproducibility of results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors provide a new approach for curriculum learning using the ZSP concept used in pedagogy. This is an interesting approach and the manuscript includes an extensive evaluation of the method in several domains. Nonetheless, I have raised several concerns, such as the distance between the theory of the paper and the concrete practical variant, the generality of the method considering the limited number of tasks and generalisation performance beyond the training tasks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer hygW
content.comment:
Thank you for carefully reviewing our paper! We greatly appreciate your feedback. Please see below our responses to your comments.

-----
**1. One of my concerns about this work is the distance between the theory (including the ZPD concept) and the actual practical algorithm used in empirical evaluations… What if there are unsolvable tasks in the task space, i.e. the goals are unreachable from a certain initial state?**
	
We appreciate the concern raised by the reviewer. We agree that the proposed curriculum is derived by analyzing simple learning settings. However, in Section 3.3, we have provided a detailed step-by-step discussion on how our curriculum can be applied in increasingly complex settings. We still believe there is a utility in analyzing simple learning settings as it provides conceptual clarity, and we do hope that one will be able to extend this analysis in future works.

The reviewer raises an interesting point regarding the unsolvable tasks in the task space. In some of our initial experiments with tabular environments, we actually conducted an experiment where 50% of the tasks were unsolvable. In this experiment, the correct PoS* is 1 for solvable tasks and the correct PoS* is 0 for unsolvable tasks. We noticed that even if we set PoS*=1 for all the tasks, the curriculum strategy is quite robust — it would avoid picking unsolvable tasks in any case because their value w.r.t. Eq. 1 equals 0 as PoS_t=0. In the final version of the paper, we will add a discussion about this point in Section 3.3. We would also like to mention that without any domain knowledge, one can assume that all the tasks are solvable in a given environment and this assumption doesn’t distance the method from the ZPD theory. It would also be interesting to infer PoS* values automatically during the training process (e.g., by training a population of agents).

-----

**2. Another weakness is that all environments seem to include only a limited |Sinit|  (in the order of hundreds, except BasicKarell if I understand correctly).**

The closely related work on multi-task contextual RL that uses fixed pools is the SPaCE method; their experimental setup considered pool sizes up to a few hundred tasks. In our work, we have additionally included the BasicKarel environment with 24,000 discrete tasks that offer a few order magnitudes larger pool size. It would indeed be interesting to extend our method in settings with infinite pool sizes; this would require us to exploit some form of similarity between tasks during the selection process.

-----

**3. It is unclear whether the agents would generalise to new tasks that they have not seen during training.**

In Figure 8 of Appendix C.4, we have reported the performance of the trained agents on new test sets (sampled from the task space), different from the training sets used in the training process.

-----

**4. I’d also be interested to see the curriculum visualisation of ProCuRL-env, which is closer to the theory.**

In the final version of the paper, we will update the curriculum visualization plots in Figures 4 and 5 by incorporating ProCuRL-env. Below, we provide initial tables with the context evolution of ProCuRL-env for the environments PointMass-s and BasicKarel. 

**Context Evolution of ProCuRL-env: PointMass-s**

| C-GateWidth | $5.3$ | $5.0$ | $3.7$ | 
| C-Friction | $1.7$ | $1.8$ | $1.7$ | 

**Context Evolution of ProCuRL-env: BasicKarel**

| Context | 0.25M | 0.5M | 1M | 
| ----- | --- | --- | --- | 
| C-TrajLength | $4.40$ | $4.80$ | $5.30$ | 
| C-MarkerAction | $0.50$ | $0.59$ | $0.75$ | 
| C-DistractorMarker | $0.49$ | $0.51$ | $0.56$ | 
| C-Walls | $6.01$ | $6.02$ | $6.10$ | 

-----

**5. The method proposed in this work presents a great resemblance to some of the Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) methods, which also belong to the field of Curriculum Learning … I thus think these connections need to be acknowledged and prior work properly cited.**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the connection to the Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) methods. We will appropriately acknowledge the prior work on UED methods and discuss its connection with our proposed curriculum in the final version of the paper.

-----
**6. (Minor) shouldn’t the \xi also include the rewards in their notation?**

Thanks for pointing this out. We had omitted the rewards here since we were originally writing the notation for a goal-based setting where the reward values are implicitly encoded in the trajectory. We will update this in the final version of the paper accordingly.

-----

We hope that our responses can address your concerns and are helpful in improving your rating. If you have any other comments or feedback, please let us know! We will be happy to provide further responses. We are looking forward to hearing back from you! Thank you again for the review.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an automated curriculum learning strategy based on the idea of Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), where the tasks are meant to be neither too hard nor too easy.

The strategy, named ProCuRL, consists of choosing tasks maximizing $currentPerformance * (bestPerformance - currentPerformance)$

Authors provide a mathematical argumentation behind using such a rule under the assumptions of:

1. Independent tasks: learning on one task doesn't affect policy parameters used in other tasks
2. Task being described by the initial state, with {0, 1} reward
3. A gradient-based like rule with a single parameter for a given task

Due to practical limitations, the actual method that is tested involves sampling from a softmax distribution, assuming the best possible score on any task is 1, and (optionally) estimating the current performance using (normalised) value functions.

The method is evaluated on a set of 5 tasks, and the performance is compared to SPaCE, SPDL, and uniform task-sampling strategy, with authors claiming performance improvements over the other methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

The empirical results are convincing and pointing to improvement over the baselines.

## Weaknesses

The notation of the paper is very confusing, to the point I am not sure I understand (the mathematical motivation part of) the paper. The same letter $\theta$ is used for "parameters" (from $R^d$) and "performance on tasks" (from $[0, 1]^{|tasks|}$). At some point one is implicitly interpreted as the other, despite different meanings and incompatible types.

This is further confusing as derivatives over scores are calculated, but given that the same object is interpreted as the parameters, which the method controls, so to optimize the "score=parameter" surely just setting the parameters to 1 (corresponding to always solving the task) would solve the posed optimization problem.

Even when considered alone, the gradient-based rule seems unintuitive: authors assume to have access to the final/target parameter $\theta^*$ and move the current parameter towards final with various strengths $\alpha, \beta$, depending on whether the current trajectory succeeded in solving the tasks.

The setting chosen by authors for motivating the work seems arbitrary and unrealistic: all currently published methods rely on the network sharing parameters between tasks.

The mathematical methods used to prove the case for ProCuRL are not interesting on their own.

The claim about the proposed method being in any way closer to the ZPD concept than the previous literature is an overstatement. It's not clear how authors interpret that statement, given that the manuscript makes no reference to ZPD when defining their method.

In its final formulation, the method effectively amounts to (softly) prefer tasks on which agent's performance (modeled by the agent) is close to 0.5, which doesn't, actually, follow ZPD: at the beginning of training, tasks with 0.5 success rate may be too hard for the agent, and at the end, they may be too easy.

The evaluation of ProCuRL-Env, which doesn't take into account the environment frames used for estimating the current performance of the agent and choose better tasks is not fair.

## Suggestions

It would be good to include a baseline based on goal relabeling, e.g VDS [1], or HER [2].

[1]: Zhang et al. [Automatic Curriculum Learning through Value Disagreement](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/file/566f0ea4f6c2e947f36795c8f58ba901-Paper.pdf)

[2]: Andrychowicz et al. [Hindsight Experience Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.01495)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As mentioned above, my biggest concern about the work is the clarity of the writing, which makes it hard for me to understand the motivation part of the paper.

While I doubt the exact formulation that authors use for choosing the tasks was used in previous literature, I don't consider prioritizing the tasks according to $V(s) * (1- V(s))$ to be particularly novel nor efficient for general task distributions, despite the encouraging results presented by the authors in the experimental section.

I consider the work reproducible (in the same task distributions).
content.summary_of_the_review:
I find the motivation part of the work highly confusing.

The actual method that is derived seems to only be applicable when the median (in the absolute scale) performance task is the best one to use over the course of training, which is restrictive. Despite that, authors make an ungrounded, strong claim about their method being closer to the ZPD concept than any published work.

In my mind, at least the mathematical motivation section needs a rewrite before the work could be published at ICLR.

edit: after discussion with the authors I understood a paper a little bit better and decreased the score from 5 to 3.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6MFC - Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for carefully reviewing our paper! We greatly appreciate your feedback. Please see below our responses to your comments.

-----
**1. The notation of the paper is very confusing, to the point I am not sure I understand (the mathematical motivation part of) the paper.**

> The same letter $\theta$ is used for "parameters" (from $\mathbb{R}^d$) and "performance on tasks" (from $[0,1]^{\text{tasks}}$).

In the general goal-based setting, each knowledge "parameter" $\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is mapped to a policy $\pi_\theta: \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \to [0,1]$, which in turn defines a vector of "performance on tasks" $\text{PoS}_\theta = V^{\pi_\theta} \in [0,1]^{\mathcal{S}_\text{init}}$. The learner update happens in the "parameter" space $\Theta$. In Section 3.2.1, we consider a specific learning setting where we abstract out the policy $\pi_\theta$ and directly map the "parameter" $\theta$ to a vector of "performance on tasks" $\text{PoS}_\theta$. For this specific setting, we choose the parameter space as $\Theta = [0,1]^{\mathcal{S}_\text{init}}$ (where $d = \mathcal{S}_\text{init}$) and define $\text{PoS}_\theta = \theta$. Thus, the update in the "parameter" $\theta$ is equivalent to the update in the "performance on tasks" $\text{PoS}_\theta$. We will clarify this further in the final version of the paper. 

> This is further confusing as derivatives over scores are calculated, but given that the same object is interpreted as the parameters, which the method controls, so to optimize the "score=parameter" surely just setting the parameters to 1 (corresponding to always solving the task) would solve the posed optimization problem.

At step $t$, we want to move the vector $\theta_t = PoS_{\theta_{t}}$ closer to $\theta^* = PoS_{\theta*}$ to maximize the uniform performance over the task space. However, this is not possible in a single step since by picking a task $s$ only the corresponding component gets updated by $\alpha \cdot (\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$ or $\beta \cdot (\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$. Thus, we need to pick a task with appropriate success scores (w.r.t. $\theta^*$ and $\theta_t$) to maximize the progress of $\theta_t$ towards $\theta^*$. 

> Even when considered alone, the gradient-based rule seems unintuitive: authors assume to have access to the final/target parameter $\theta^*$.

The parameter update of the abstract agent model (used in our analysis) involves the term $(\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s]) = (\text{PoS}^*[s] - \text{PoS}_t[s])$ that is equal to the maximum possible success score improvement for the picked task $s$. We designed this update rule to capture the ZPD concept: the learning progress is maximized when the learner is presented with tasks that are “not too easy” and “not too hard”. In particular, when picking a task that is “too easy”, the progress in $\theta_t$ towards $\theta^*$ is minimal since $(\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$ is low. Similarly, when picking a task that is “too hard” (assuming the agent fails in the task and $\beta$ is close to $0$), the progress in $\theta_t$ towards $\theta^*$ is minimal since $\beta \cdot (\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$ is low. We will clarify this further in the final version of the paper. Crucially, we note that our final curriculum strategies in Section 3.3 do not require access to the target parameter $\theta^*$ or $\text{PoS}^*$ values. 

> Conceptual contribution of the abstract learner update.

One way to reason about the ZPD concept, when applied in terms of learning progress, is that progress is maximized when the learner is presented with tasks that lie in the proximal zone, i.e., tasks are “not too easy” and “not too hard”. To capture this conception, we need an appropriate update rule for the learner. To this end, we designed the learner update rule in Section 3.2.1 that aligns with this conception. 


**2. The setting chosen by authors for motivating the work seems arbitrary and unrealistic: all currently published methods rely on the network sharing parameters between tasks.**

Theorems 1/2 in Section 3.2 basically provide a theoretical basis to derive our curriculum strategy ProCuRL in Eq. 1. We agree that the proposed curriculum is derived by analyzing simple learning settings, such as contextual bandit problems with REINFORCE agent. We still believe there is a utility in analyzing simple learning settings as it provides conceptual clarity. In Section 3.3, we have provided a detailed step-by-step discussion on how our curriculum can be applied in practice to increasingly complex settings. 

Importantly, we have extensively evaluated the performance of our curriculum strategy in popular deep RL environments used in state-of-the-art works and demonstrated its effectiveness.

-----
(the response is continued in Part 2)

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1102 by Reviewer 6FMC

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6MFC - Part 2
content.comment:
(continuation of the response from Part 1)

-----

**3. The claim about the proposed method being in any way closer to the ZPD concept than the previous literature is an overstatement. It's not clear how authors interpret that statement, given that the manuscript makes no reference to ZPD when defining their method.**

Thank you for the comment. The connection between our proposed curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 and the ZPD concept is highlighted in Section 3.2.1. One conception of ZPD, when applied in terms of learning progress, is that progress is maximized when the learner is presented with tasks that lie in ZPD, i.e., “not too easy” and “not too hard”. To capture this conception, we designed the update rule in Section 3.2.1. In particular, when picking a task that is “too easy”, the progress in $\theta_t$ towards $\theta^*$ is minimal since $(\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$ is low. Similarly, when picking a task that is “too hard” (assuming the agent fails in the task and $\beta$ is close to $0$), the progress in $\theta_t$ towards $\theta^*$ is minimal since $\beta \cdot (\theta^*[s] - \theta_t[s])$ is low. We will further highlight the connections in the final version of the paper.

-----

**4. In its final formulation, the method effectively amounts to (softly) prefer tasks on which agent's performance (modeled by the agent) is close to 0.5, which doesn't, actually, follow ZPD … The actual method that is derived seems to only be applicable when the median (in the absolute scale) performance task is the best one to use over the course of training**

Here we provide some clarification related to the curriculum strategy in Eq. 1. The curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 would pick a task as per the objective in the equation, and we do not require the PoS_t(s) value of the picked task to be the median or have a specific value of 0.5. In fact, as per Theorems 1/2, our analysis shows that picking tasks based on the curriculum strategy given in Eq. 1 maximizes the expected improvement to the training objective in Eq. 2. We will further clarify this point in the final version of the paper. 

-----
**5. The evaluation of ProCuRL-Env, which doesn't take into account the environment frames used for estimating the current performance of the agent and choose better tasks is not fair.**

We kindly refer the reviewer to check Figure 3, where we systematically compare different strategies in terms of three metrics: performance, environment steps, and clock time. Moreover, as mentioned in Section 3.3, the primary motivation for introducing ProCuRL-Val over ProCuRL-Env is to remove the sample inefficiency of computing $PoS_t$ values using rollouts and replacing them with $V_t$ values from the critic network. 

-----

**6. It would be good to include a baseline based on goal relabeling, e.g VDS [1], or HER [2].**

In our experiments, we primarily focused on state-of-the-art baselines that can operate on a fixed pool of tasks (without any task generation), and included SPaCE and SPDL strategies that have been recently proposed for the multi-task / contextual RL settings. We will add a further discussion about VDS, HER, and related techniques in the paper.

-----

We hope that our responses can address your concerns and are helpful in improving your rating. If you have any other comments or feedback, please let us know! We will be happy to provide further responses. We are looking forward to hearing back from you! Thank you again for the review.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer 6MFC - Part 2

content.title: Thank you for explanations
content.comment:
1. I thank the authors for the detailed explanation of the mathematical part of the paper. Let me try to rephrase their explanation to make sure I understood it.

a. We assume that there is a single parameter per task and that there is a simple function (which is meant to behave like identity, but maps from $\mathcal{R}$ to $[0, 1]$) mapping a parameter to the performance on that task. I will appreciate reading the more formalized version once it's ready.

b. Then, we devise an update rule which assumes that it updates a single task's parameter along the direction to the optimal one, and keeps the remaining ones fixed.

c. We claim that out of the update rules of the form proposed by us (with a particular choice of $\alpha$ and $\beta$), the optimal choice of the next task to update is one which maximizes $p (p^* - p)$.

d. As such, we argue for the main method which uses value function to estimate the performance and assumes optimal performance to be 1.

With this understanding, I stand by most of the critical comments I made. Below I rephrase them and point out where the authors' response didn't address the original concern that I had.

2. I understand the authors' argument for their method based on the derivation (move from step c to d above), but I find this argument weak: the theoretical derivation is made in the setting that's so much different from the real-life scenario (mostly: a direct mapping between parameters and performance and access to the value of the perfect performance=parameter during optimization) that the fact that some method works in this simplified setting doesn't tell us much about the performance of the full method.

Note that it doesn't mean that I believe the full method won't work (as I mentioned, the experimental results are rather encouraging), but rather that the argumentation is weak; I disagree with the statements about the full method being "derived from basic principles".

3. Thank you for explaining your interpretation of ZPD, which I was missing in the paper. As the argumentation is based on the unrealistic assumptions, I am not convinced that the full method actually follows ZPD (or actually, I'm convinced that it doesn't, as argued below), as in the full method you don't have access to $theta^*$ (in terms of parameters) and are not able to make statements directly relating change in parameters and performance improvements.

Furthermore, I don't find the strength of your argument any greater than the arguments presented in the past literature arguing that various methods follow ZPD.

4. "we do not require the $PoS_t(s)$ value of the picked task to be the median or have a specific value of 0.5.". I find that your comment doesn't address my concern. I understand that you don't always select the task with median performance, but your density function expressing the "expected utility of the task" is maximized by the task of median performance. My argument tries to portray a situation where the median performance task is not the one of the highest utility: a situation where ProCuRL will make unoptimal decisions.

5. Your comment ("look at Figure 3") doesn't address my concern. I understand that you evaluated ProCuRL-Env in a couple of settings with varying "evaluation budget", but I consider showing the performance on the plot / table with X = number of steps and Y = performance, where there has been other interactions with the environment happening outside of the ones portrayed on the X axis unfair.

I hope it won't come with a significant disappointment that in the view of my current understanding of the paper, I decreased my score to "reject" as I cannot apply the benefit of the doubt anymore.

content.title: Concrete example
content.comment:
Thank you for the clarifying comment. I mean a situation like this:

1. it's the beginning of the training, and we're discussing the full method (no access to ground truth parameter -> performance)
2. there is 5 tasks available, with corresponding value functions / probabilities of success 0., 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, and 0.4.
3. the sampling weight for choosing the last (0.4) task is higher than the others, despite it being significantly easier. This disagrees with my understanding of ZPD, where the task closer to a medium performance should be chosen.

replying_to: Replying to Concrete example

content.title: Re. Concrete Example
content.comment:
Thank you for the follow-up and for sharing this example. We greatly appreciate the reviewer's feedback. We would like to share a few thoughts:

- First, when PoS* values are simply set to 1.0 when applying Eq. 1, it could pick tasks that are suboptimal for some scenarios as presented by the reviewer.
- Second, our claim about the optimality of Eq. 1 holds only under the two settings considered in Section 3.2. More concretely, these settings for Theorems 1/2 assume knowledge of PoS*, assume independent tasks with goal-based rewards, and have specific learner update rules. Under these settings, picking tasks w.r.t. Eq. 1 is equivalent to greedily optimizing the training objective in Eq. 2.
- Third, when applying our curriculum strategy in deep RL environments, our design of setting PoS* values to 1.0 led to strong performance. However, there are alternative choices in estimating PoS* values during the training process – for instance, in Section 3.3, we have suggested a variant where PoS* is estimated using top $K$\% rollouts obtained by executing the current policy $\pi_t$ starting from $s$.

replying_to: Replying to Re. Concrete Example

content.title: a little more nuance
content.comment:
Thank you for the comments. I agree with your statements, but wanted to offer one more detailed point:

the issue I mentioned (in the full setting with value function, so not the one where you are claiming optimality on) cannot be fully circumvented by a smart fixed choice of PoS*.

While at the beginning of the training the distribution of scores / value estimates would be as proposed above, it is expected that it'll change as the training progresses. Even if the practitioner chose PoS*=0.03 (which would prioritize the "medium performance tasks" at the beginning of the training) (even though it seems weird given the interpretation of PoS* as the best possible score), it would likely be a wrong choice by the end of training where the running scores of the agents are higher.

replying_to: Replying to a little more nuance

content.title: Re. a little more nuance
content.comment:
We agree that setting a fixed value of PoS*(s) for all the tasks could be problematic. 

In the previous response, the alternative choice we suggested would estimate PoS*(s) separately for each task $s \in S_{init}$ at step $t$. One possible way to do this is to estimate PoS*(s) at step $t$ using top $K$\% rollouts obtained by executing the current policy $\pi_t$ starting from each $s$. So, this is similar in spirit to computing PoS_t(s) at time $t$ that uses $100$\% of the obtained rollouts for estimation. This way, PoS*(s) values are specific to each task $s$, and they will be at least as high as PoS_t(s) values at any step $t$.  

Alternatively, one could also consider population-based methods where multiple critic networks are used to estimate PoS_t(s) and PoS*(s) values, and top $K$\% network values are used for PoS*(s) estimation.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper mainly considers curriculum learning in goal-based reinforcement learning. 
A fixed set of curriculum tasks is defined by a set of initial states, and the algorithm can sample tasks from the set at every step. The final goal is to maximize performance with respect to a uniform distribution of tasks (which is known). Specifically, motivated by the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in educational psychology, the authors propose a curriculum strategy by choosing tasks of medium difficulty. The difficulty is measured by a negative quadratic term of the value function. Then the authors justify a training objective and an update rule w.r.t. the agent parameters by showing two specific settings. Besides, the authors provide solutions to some practical issues. The experiments are based on maze environments and robotic control environments and show a leading performance against the state-of-the-art curriculum algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- Novelty: the authors provide a new self-paced curriculum learning objective.

- Empirical evaluation: This paper has a nice experimental part, with four representative environments, multiple baselines, and ablation studies in terms of \beta and noise.

- Writing: This paper has a good flow to present the motivation and the solution.

However, I have several concerns here:
- Literature: the authors should discuss and highlight the difference between ProCuRL and other related algorithms, like SPCL and SPACE. Since the main part of the related work just introduces other works.

- Methodology

	-  It is unclear to me where Eq.1 comes from. To my understanding, $PoS^*$ is a constant when $S_{init}$ is given. Then, when $PoS_t = 0.5 \times PoS^*$, the maximization is obtained. So Eq.1 implicitly assumes that achieving the half of value function is the medium difficulty, which is not obvious in the experimental environments. In this case, what if we maximize $PoS_t \dot (\gamma_1 PoS^* - \gamma_ 2 PoS_t)$ with different $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$.

	- Then, it is also unclear to me the link between Eq.1 and Eq.2. Does it mean that when following curriculum strategy as Eq.1, the objective in Eq.2 is maximized?
	- It is not obvious how to use the smooth condition in [1]. Eq.7 in [1] shows the smooth condition, however, the \lambda in [1] does not have the same meaning as \theta in this paper. Since intuitively, the case that $\theta$ is approaching $\theta^*$ does not mean that $V^\theta$ is approaching $V^{\theta^*}$ 
	- The $s_t$ in the left term of Eq.1, Eq.3, Eq.4, and Eq.5 does not match line 13 in Algorithm 2. It may be a typo but cause some confusing points.
	- $\theta_t$ is a learned parameter in PPO. So $V_t$ might introduce an estimation error during training. For example, if $V_t$ is of high variance, the curriculum strategy will fail.

- Theoretical justification
	- Just as stated in the conclusion part, the justification is far away from the implementation, which makes this paper less attractive.

content.title: Response to Reviewer CJZ3 - Part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for carefully reviewing our paper! We greatly appreciate your feedback. Please see below our responses to your comments.

-----
**1. The authors should discuss and highlight the difference between ProCuRL and other related algorithms, like SPDL and SPaCE.**

In Section 1.1, the paragraph “Curriculum strategies based on self-paced learning (SPL)” primarily discusses SPDL and SPaCE. As suggested by the reviewer, we will include more technical details of these curriculum strategies in the final version of the paper. For example, for SPDL, we will add information on the optimization problem solved at each step to pick a task; for SPaCE, we will add details on how differences in current/previous critic values are used at each step to pick a task. In Appendix C.3, we have also provided some additional information on hyperparameters for SPDL and SPaCE.

-----

**2. It is unclear to me where Eq.1 comes from… If the curriculum strategy is just shown in Eq.1, the novelty is inadequate… To my understanding, $PoS^\*$ is a constant when $S_{init}$ is given. Then, when $PoS_t = 0.5 \times PoS^\*$, the maximization is obtained… In this case, what if we maximize $PoS_t (\gamma_1 PoS^\* - \gamma_2 PoS_t)$ with different $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$.**

The curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 is based on the insights from Theorems 1/2 (Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2), where we analyzed simple learning settings to derive a curriculum strategy that optimizes the training objective in Eq. 2. We further clarify this point in response 3. below where we discuss a link between the curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 and the training objective in Eq. 2.

Theorems 1/2 and short texts following them highlight how we arrived at the specific form of curriculum strategy in Eq 1. If we would not consider the simplified learning settings for our analysis (e.g., have dependent tasks), we will get a more complex form of curriculum strategy. In fact, we did these simplifications to have a curriculum strategy that doesn't require any domain-specific hyperparameters. As highlighted in contribution III., our curriculum strategy can be easily integrated with deep RL frameworks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. It would also be interesting to extend the curriculum strategy with additional hyperparameters by analyzing more complex learning settings.

Nevertheless, the reviewer has made an interesting suggestion to parameterize our curriculum with $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$. As suggested, we did some additional experiments by considering the following range of $\gamma2 / \gamma1$ = {0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4}. Our default curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 essentially corresponds to $\gamma2 / \gamma1 = 1.0$. In the following table, we present initial results for the environments PointMass-s and BasicKarel.

**Performance of ProCuRL-val w.r.t. $\gamma2 / \gamma1$: PointMass-s**

| $\gamma2 / \gamma1$ | 0.25M | 0.5M | 1M | 
| ----- | --- | --- | --- | 
| 0.6 | $0.33 \pm 0.07$ | $0.50 \pm 0.07$ | $0.55 \pm 0.06$ | 
| 0.8 | $0.26 \pm 0.07$ | $0.43 \pm 0.08$ | $0.55 \pm 0.09$ | 
| 1.0 | $0.48 \pm 0.07$ | $0.64 \pm 0.08$ | $0.71 \pm 0.09$ | 
| 1.2 | $0.42 \pm 0.09$ | $0.55 \pm 0.09$ | $0.65 \pm 0.08$ |
| 1.4 | $0.39 \pm 0.08$ | $0.59 \pm 0.08$ | $0.59 \pm 0.07$ |


**Performance of ProCuRL-val w.r.t. $\gamma2 / \gamma1$: BasicKarel**

| $\gamma2 / \gamma1$ | 0.25M | 0.5M | 1M | 
| ----- | --- | --- | --- | 
| 0.6 | $0.08 \pm 0.02$ | $0.21 \pm 0.03$ | $0.41 \pm 0.04$ | 
| 0.8 | $0.11 \pm 0.01$ | $0.36 \pm 0.02$ | $0.64 \pm 0.03$ | 
| 1.0 | $0.10 \pm 0.01$ | $0.38 \pm 0.01$ | $0.76 \pm 0.02$ | 
| 1.2 | $0.07 \pm 0.02$ | $0.30 \pm 0.05$ | $0.72 \pm 0.03$ |
| 1.4 | $0.04 \pm 0.01$ | $0.21 \pm 0.03$ | $0.71 \pm 0.02$ |

We will add this discussion and additional results in the final version of the paper.

-----

**3. Unclear to me the link between Eq.1 and Eq.2. Does it mean that when following curriculum strategy as Eq.1, the objective in Eq.2 is maximized?**

We have provided a link between the curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 and the training objective in Eq. 2 in short texts following Theorems 1/2 in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2. We will clarify this connection further in the final version of the paper. 

More concretely, these theorems characterize the impact of picking a task at step $t$ on the objective in Eq. 2 with the following values: (i) task’s PoS w.r.t. the target policy $\pi_{\theta^*}$ having value $p^*$ and (ii) task’s PoS w.r.t. the agent’s current policy having value $p$. For the specific learning settings considered in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2, Theorems 1/2 imply that picking tasks based on the curriculum strategy given in Eq. 1 maximizes the expected improvement to the objective in Eq. 2. We also refer the reviewer to the proofs of Theorems 1/2 in Appendix B.

-----
(the response is continued in Part 2)

content.title: Response to Reviewer CJZ3 - Part 2
content.comment:
(continuation of the response from Part 1)

-----

**4. It is not obvious how to use the smooth condition in [1]. Eq.7 in [1] shows the smooth condition, however, the $\lambda$ in [1] does not have the same meaning as $\theta$ in this paper.**

In fact, we meant to have a smoothness condition on the value function of the form $|V^{\pi_\theta} - V^{\pi_{\theta’}}| \leq ||\theta - \theta’||$. For the softmax policy parameterization in the specific setting of Section 3.2.2, the smoothness condition on the reward function provided in [1] can be translated to the smoothness condition on the value function. We will further clarify this point in the final version of the paper. 

-----

**5. The $s_t$ in the left term of Eq.1, Eq.3, Eq.4, and Eq.5 does not match line 13 in Algorithm 2.**

Thank you for pointing this out. In Eq.1 and Algorithm 1, we defined $t$ at an episodic level. However, Algorithm 2 presents the implementation of our curriculum strategy in the context of the PPO method, and here $t$ denotes an environment step. We will update Algorithm 2 to clarify this issue in the final version of the paper.

-----

**6. $\theta_t$ is a learned parameter in PPO. So $V_t$ might introduce an estimation error during training. For example, if $V_t$ is of high variance, the curriculum strategy will fail.**

Indeed, the reviewer raises an important point. Since $V_t$ values are computed using the critic network that is also learned in the process, there might be error/noise in these values. This is the motivation behind the robustness study presented in Appendix C.4. In Figure 9, we show the robustness of our curriculum strategy w.r.t. error/noise in $V_t$ values (here, we specifically inject additional noise into the estimated values).

-----

**7. Just as stated in the conclusion part, the justification is far away from the implementation, which makes this paper less attractive.**

We do appreciate the concern raised by the reviewer. In the literature, several curriculum strategies based on the concept of ZPD or learning progress have been studied as heuristics; our work proposes a theoretically justified ZPD-based curriculum strategy ProCuRL. We derived our proposed curriculum strategy by analyzing simple learning settings, such as contextual bandit problems with REINFORCE agent. We still believe there is a utility in analyzing simple learning settings as it provides conceptual clarity, and we hope that one will be able to extend this analysis to more complex learning settings in future works.

In Section 3.3, we have provided a detailed step-by-step discussion on how our curriculum can be applied in practice to increasingly complex settings. Moreover, we extensively evaluated the performance of our curriculum strategy in a variety of deep RL environments and demonstrated its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines.

-----

We hope that our responses can address your concerns and are helpful in improving your rating. If you have any other comments or feedback, please let us know! We will be happy to provide further responses. We are looking forward to hearing back from you! Thank you again for the review.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a curriculum strategy for reinforcement learning that selects initial states for the agent such that they are in the "Zone of Proximal Development" (ZPD), i.e. selecting states that are not too easy and not too hard. They formalize this concept in the context of reinforcement learning, and provide different implementations of the strategy. The paper provides experimental results on several different environments (PointMass, BasicKarel, BallCatching, and Antgoal), and show that their method performs as well or better than the baselines on most environments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- I think the paper is well motivated with the idea of ZPD. The idea of selecting a curriculum based on that concept makes sense, and the paper also does a decent enough job at formalizing this concept (although certain steps need more explanation).
- The paper runs its experiments on a fairly wide array of environments, and shows that their method is competitive or outperforms other baselines on all of those environments, even when constraining to a similar number of resources.
- The paper proposes two variants of their method, one based on policy rollouts to estimate of the "probability of success" metric, and one where the metric was computed with a function approximator value function. The paper also shows the effect of using fewer policy rollouts and getting closer to the value function based variant.

Weaknesses:
- The authors mention a result that as the pool size of available initial states increases, their method is better able to create a curriculum compared to other methods. To make this claim, they looked at the effect of pool size across different environments, but this claim would be more convincing if within the same environment, they sample different number of tasks for the pool, and show that their method does better as the pool size increases.
- The theoretical justification could be made clearer. Specifically the link between theorems 1/2 and the curriculum objectives.

Question:
- Why do the procurl-env^{2,4} methods take less time than the procurl-val method for BasicKarel?

content.title: Response to Reviewer WHtK
content.comment:
Thank you for carefully reviewing our paper! We greatly appreciate your feedback. Please see below our responses to your comments.

-----
**1. The authors mention a result that as the pool size of available initial states increases, their method is better able to create a curriculum compared to other methods.**

The main point we wanted to convey is that ProCuRL-val performs better compared to SPDL and SPaCE in terms of computational and time complexity. The effect of that is more evident as the pool size increases.
The reason is that ProCuRL-val only requires forward-pass operation on the critic-model to obtain value estimates for each task in the pool. SPDL and SPaCE not only require the same forward-pass operations, but SPDL does an additional optimization step, and SPaCE requires a task ordering step. The same effect on time complexity is expected in any environment as the number of tasks increases.

-----
**2. The theoretical justification could be made clearer. Specifically the link between theorems 1/2 and the curriculum objectives.**

In short texts following Theorems 1/2 in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2, we have provided a link between the curriculum strategy in Eq. 1 and the training objective in Eq. 2. We will clarify these points further in the final version of the paper. 

More concretely, these theorems characterize the impact of picking a task at step $t$ on the objective in Eq. 2 with the following values: (i) task’s PoS w.r.t. the target policy $\pi_{\theta^*}$ having value $p^*$ and (ii) task’s PoS w.r.t. the agent’s current policy having value $p$. For the specific learning settings considered in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2, Theorems 1/2 imply that picking tasks based on the curriculum strategy given in Eq. 1 maximizes the expected improvement to the objective in Eq. 2. We also refer the reviewer to the proofs of Theorems 1/2 in Appendix B.

-----
**3. Why do the procurl-env^{2,4} methods take less time than the procurl-val method for BasicKarel?**

To achieve the constrained budget of evaluation steps in procurl-env^{2,4}, we reduce the frequency of updating PoS_t since this is the most expensive operation for ProCuRL-env requiring additional rollouts for each task. On the other hand, ProCuRL-val updates PoS_t by using the values obtained from forward-pass on the critic model – this update happens whenever the critic model is updated (every 2048 training steps for BasicKarel). This higher frequency of updating PoS_t in ProCuRL-val is why it is slower than procurl_env^{2,4} for BasicKarel. 

We would also like to note that the relative frequency of updates for PointMass is different in comparison to BasicKarel because of very different pool sizes. Hence, the behavior in total clock times is different.

-----

We hope that our responses can address your concerns and are helpful in improving your rating. If you have any other comments or feedback, please let us know! We will be happy to provide further responses. We are looking forward to hearing back from you! Thank you again for the review.
